name: Rafael Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the season. Outside storm season, I'm at the Coastline Power yard at seven, and we're replacing wooden poles with concrete ones along the coast road, hardening the system, they call it, so it stands up better to the wind. In storm season it's sixteen-hour days for two weeks straight after a hurricane, sleeping in a church hall, getting neighbourhoods back one street at a time. I'm a second-year apprentice at 58, so I'm the one hauling and rigging while the journeymen do the hot work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twenty-two years in the army fixing trucks and generators, then eight years running maintenance at a hospital. I have my military pension, and my wife Elena and I own our house outright. When the veterans' hiring programme at Coastline came along, I took it, because after the last big storm I watched those crews work and thought, that's real service. Darnell, the journeyman I ride with, was in the navy, so we understand each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: a tool is a tool. At the yard I'd tell the young guys that no computer ever stood up a pole in a hurricane. Online I don't say much, maybe a comment on the veterans' group page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means I keep going. I finish the apprenticeship, work storm seasons until I'm 64 or 65, and retire with two pensions. Nothing in my plans moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rafael keeps going as he is, working the pole replacements and storm seasons. He'd keep using the AI chatbot now and then to read the hurricane forecasts in plain words, and keep his money exactly where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet week between storms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use a chatbot for the forecasts. How does that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before storm season I'll paste in the long forecast discussion from the weather service and ask it to tell me what it means for our stretch of coast. It does a fair job. Then I call my brother-in-law, who's been fishing these waters forty years, and he tells me what it really means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your family would you think about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter Anya, she's an accountant with two little ones. People keep telling her AI will take her job. In this picture she'd be fine, and I'd be glad for her.

S0.say: I'd say a tool is a tool, and no computer ever stood up a pole in a hurricane. Maybe a comment on the veterans' group page, but not much online.
S0.think: Privately he keeps going, finishing the apprenticeship and working storm seasons until 64 or 65. He'd retire with two pensions and nothing in his plans would move.
S0.do: Keeps going with pole replacements and storm seasons. Uses the chatbot now and then to explain hurricane forecasts in plain words and leaves his money where it is.
S0.feel: Calm, like a quiet week between storms.
S0.quote: Then I call my brother-in-law, who's been fishing these waters forty years, and he tells me what it really means.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael frames his work as service, a thread from the army to storm crews. He uses AI occasionally and sensibly but trusts experienced people more. His thoughts turn quickly to his daughter's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how it's always been: new equipment comes, you train on it, you do the job. The army changed our gear every few years. I'd tell the young guys to stop whining and go to the training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. I'm not the fastest learner, but I'm disciplined, and I'll sit through a manual. Line work will change a bit, drones for patrols after storms, maybe smarter switches, and I can live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rafael would go to every company training on new storm-assessment tools once the first crews had tried them. He'd use AI a little more, asking it to quiz him before his apprenticeship tests. He'd keep putting a share of his pay into savings as he does now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit tired at the thought of more classroom time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: After a hurricane, what would change if drones did the patrols?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd know which streets are worst before we roll out, instead of driving round in the dark. Last year, Darnell and I spent four hours finding a single broken crossarm behind a strip mall. A drone would have seen it in five minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say the young guys should stop whining. Is that fair if they've got thirty years left and you've got six?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. They've got more on the line than me. But whining doesn't help anyone, training does. I'd tell them that, and then I'd help them study, because that's what the sergeants did for me.

S1.say: I'd say new equipment comes, you train on it and you do the job, as the army changed gear every few years. I'd tell the young guys to stop whining and go to the training.
S1.think: Privately he'd be fine: not a fast learner but disciplined enough to sit through a manual. Drones and smarter switches would change line work a bit, and he can live with that.
S1.do: Attends company training on new storm-assessment tools once the first crews have tried them. Uses AI a little more to quiz himself before apprenticeship tests and keeps saving part of his pay.
S1.feel: Calm, a little tired at the thought of more classroom time.
S1.quote: Last year, Darnell and I spent four hours finding a single broken crossarm behind a strip mall.
S1.fieldNote: His military habits shape his attitude: train, then do the job. When the gap between his stake and younger workers' was named, he accepted it gracefully and offered to help them study. He sees clear practical gains from drones in storm work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is reckless, rushing something like this out in two years. In public I'd say companies should be free to build what they want, but they should answer for what happens to the people they put out of work. I'd say it at the veterans' hall and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm all right. I've got the army pension, the house is paid off, and Elena and I live simply. What gets me is Anya and her family, and the young guys on my crew with mortgages. I've had orders change overnight before, but I've never seen a whole country's orders change at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rafael would keep working storm seasons as long as Coastline needed people, because robots won't be ready for every flooded street on day one. He'd put an extra 500 a month into savings to help Anya if her job went, and offer to help pay for his grandchildren's schooling. If the robots took the crews, he'd retire at 60 without complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for myself, for the people I'm responsible for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what does the short time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can't finish the apprenticeship, and that annoys me, I don't like leaving a job half done. But mainly it means Anya has no time to change course. With two years, all I can do is be ready to help her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the young guys on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as I'd tell a new private: get your money in order, lean on each other, and do the next job in front of you. And if they need a place to stay, our spare room's empty since the kids left.

S2.say: I'd say it's reckless to rush something like this out in two years. Companies should be free to build, but they should answer for what happens to the people they put out of work.
S2.think: Privately he's all right, with his army pension, a paid-off house and simple living. What troubles him is his daughter's family and young crewmates with mortgages, as a whole country's orders change at once.
S2.do: Keeps working storm seasons as long as Coastline needs people, and puts an extra 500 a month aside to help his daughter if her job goes. Offers to help pay for his grandchildren's schooling and retires at 60 if robots take the crews.
S2.feel: Uneasy, not for himself but for those he feels responsible for.
S2.quote: I've had orders change overnight before, but I've never seen a whole country's orders change at once.
S2.fieldNote: Rafael balances free-market views with a demand that companies answer for the harm they cause. His security makes him calm about himself; his unease is about duty to family and crew. Two years mostly takes away his daughter's time to change course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fast, but a disciplined person can get ready. At the yard I'd tell people to make a plan now, not in year four. At church I'd say families should talk about it around the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gets me my journeyman card and a few good storm seasons. I'd be 63 when it arrives, and I'd step back then. Anya would have time to retrain, and that's my main relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rafael would finish his apprenticeship and work as a journeyman until about 63. He'd take any training Coastline offered on working alongside robots in storm restoration, after watching how the first crews got on. He'd sit down with Anya and help her think through a move into a different line of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's a long deployment, not an ambush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of move would you suggest for Anya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know her world well enough. Maybe something where people trust a face, like advising small businesses. I'd mostly listen, and offer to help pay for a course if she needed one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to be on storm crews in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they'd have me, yes. I imagine robots doing the climbing and somebody like me directing traffic, checking the work, talking to the people standing in their yards. Someone has to tell a scared family when their lights are coming back.

S3.say: I'd say five years is fast but a disciplined person can get ready. I'd tell people to make a plan now and say families should talk it through around the table.
S3.think: Privately five years gets him his journeyman card and a few storm seasons before stepping back at 63. His main relief is that his daughter would have time to retrain.
S3.do: Finishes his apprenticeship and works as a journeyman until about 63. Takes Coastline training on working alongside robots once early crews have tried it, and helps his daughter plan a move into different work.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steady, like a long deployment rather than an ambush.
S3.quote: Someone has to tell a scared family when their lights are coming back.
S3.fieldNote: Rafael's military metaphors help him sort the scenarios: five years is a deployment, two is an ambush. He admits he doesn't know his daughter's field well enough to advise her. He sees a lasting human role in reassuring families after storms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't prepare has only themselves to blame. That sounds hard, but it's what I believe. At the yard I'd say get your training done and your house in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it hardly touches me. I'd retire at 64 or 65, a couple of years before it arrives, with two pensions. My job would be to help my family use the decade well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rafael keeps going with his plan: journeyman card, storm seasons, retire around 64. He'd help Anya pay for any retraining she wanted and encourage his son Pavel, a firefighter, to keep his skills sharp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. This one feels like a plan, not a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years feel compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is an ambush. Ten years is a campaign you can plan for. I'd sleep fine with ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone who doesn't prepare has only themselves to blame. What about people who can't afford to prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair, and I'll take that back a little. Some folks are living paycheque to paycheque. For them I'd want the companies and churches to step up with training and apprenticeships, rather than just handing out cheques.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't prepare has only themselves to blame. At the yard I'd tell people to get their training done and their house in order.
S4.think: Privately it hardly touches him, since he'd retire at 64 or 65 with two pensions. His role would be helping his family use the decade well.
S4.do: Keeps going with his plan of journeyman card, storm seasons and retiring around 64. Helps his daughter pay for retraining and encourages his son, a firefighter, to keep his skills sharp.
S4.feel: Calm, since this feels like a plan rather than a crisis.
S4.quote: Ten years is a campaign you can plan for.
S4.fieldNote: His first answer was hard-line about personal responsibility, but he softened when asked about people who can't afford to prepare. His preferred help is training and apprenticeships from companies and churches rather than cash. Ten years lets him focus entirely on his family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be fine, but Anya and the young guys on my crew would have no time at all. What would help is companies being made to answer for the people they put out of work, paying for real training and apprenticeships, and churches and families pulling together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about storms. Every one of these pictures still has hurricanes. Whatever's climbing the poles, somebody has to decide which hospital gets power first, and I'd want that to be a person who has to look those families in the eye.

headlineQuote: Somebody has to decide which hospital gets power first, and I'd want that to be a person who has to look those families in the eye.
portrait: Rafael Petrov spent 22 years fixing army trucks and eight running hospital maintenance before joining Coastline Power's storm crews through a veterans' hiring programme at 55. He sees line work as service, uses AI now and then to read hurricane forecasts, and trusts experienced people more than machines. With a military pension and a paid-off house, he's secure, so his concern is duty to his daughter, his grandchildren and young crewmates. He calls the two-year picture an ambush and the ten-year one a campaign, and softens his tough line on personal responsibility when pressed.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his daughter and the young workers on his crew would have no time to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: Companies being made to answer for the people they put out of work by paying for training and apprenticeships, with churches and families pulling together.
